lead.en: Hawkins-style overlay: one line per year, x-axis = month, colour = year (turbo palette, oldest → youngest). Most-recent year rendered in bold amber on top.
lead.fr: Hawkins-style overlay: one line per year, x-axis = month, colour = year (turbo palette, oldest → youngest). Most-recent year rendered in bold amber on top.

body.en:
**Purpose.** Displays all years of observed monthly climate as individual lines so users can visually identify shifts in seasonal amplitude, timing, and interannual variability over the full record. Primary use case: framing a climate rationale by showing whether the recent climate is detectably different from the baseline decades.

**How to read it.** Lines shifting toward the warm (or wet) end in recent years indicate a long-term trend. Widening of the line envelope signals increasing interannual variability. The most-recent year sits in amber on top so it stays visible against the historical envelope. For PTOT, toggle **Anomaly as %** to remove the absolute-mm dependence on the country's overall rainfall regime — anomalies expressed as % of baseline are easier to compare across wet vs. dry climates.

**Methods.** Source data: CHIRPS v3 precipitation + CHIRTS-ERA5 temperature, admin-0 monthly aggregates (`adm0_obs.parquet`). Anomalies are simple departures from the per-month baseline mean over the user-selected window (WMO 1991–2020 by default; CMIP6-aligned 1995–2014 optional). Decade mean lines are arithmetic means, **not** trend estimates — incomplete decades (e.g. the 2020s) are flagged with `(n=N)` in the legend. The optional ±σ band paints monthly inter-annual standard deviation around the decade mean.

**Citations.** Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020). See [References](#references).

body.en:
**Purpose.** Stacked kernel-density curves of monthly anomaly values per decade. The view answers a question that line plots and tables can't: *is the distribution of monthly anomalies shifting (mean change) and/or broadening (variance change) over time?* Useful for extreme-event narratives — "the right tail of the distribution is getting heavier" is a precise way to talk about increasing hot months or wet months.

**How to read it.** Curves shifting **right** = warmer (or wetter) decades. Curves becoming **broader / flatter** = higher variability. Curves becoming **narrower / taller** = more consistent. For PTOT with "All months" selected, the distribution can appear bimodal — that's real: it reflects dry-season months clustered near zero anomaly and wet-season months in a longer tail. Use the season filter to isolate one regime.

**Methods.** Epanechnikov kernel density estimation on monthly anomalies (vs. selected baseline). Bandwidth from **Silverman's rule** per decade — `0.9 × min(σ, IQR/1.34) × n^−0.2` — so each decade gets its own data-adaptive smoothing. Curves are normalised to unit peak height per decade for visual stacking; **heights are comparable, areas are not** — partial decades (4–5 years of the 2020s) look as "tall" as full decades. A bandwidth floor (0.1 °C for temperature, 2 mm for precipitation) prevents degenerate output on short series.

**Citations.** Silverman (1986); Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020). See [References](#references).

lead.en: Faithful to the NASA/Hawkins spiral: **radius = anomaly** (centre = 0°C baseline, outward = warmer), **colour = anomaly** (blue = below baseline, red = above). All years drawn simultaneously — old cool years cluster near the baseline ring, recent warm years push outward. Jan at top, clockwise.
lead.fr: Faithful to the NASA/Hawkins spiral: **radius = anomaly** (centre = 0°C baseline, outward = warmer), **colour = anomaly** (blue = below baseline, red = above). All years drawn simultaneously — old cool years cluster near the baseline ring, recent warm years push outward. Jan at top, clockwise.

body.en:
**Purpose.** Polar-coordinate view where each year is a ring and the ring's radius encodes that year's monthly anomalies. Years above baseline push outward; years below push inward. The full record appears simultaneously — a tightening or expanding spiral is the signature visual of accumulating warming.

**How to read it.** Rings near the central baseline ring = near-normal years. Rings consistently pushed outward (warm/wet) or inward (cool/dry) indicate anomalous years. Recent years (highlighted in amber by default) clustering at larger radii than early years is the warming signal. For temperature, reference rings at +1.5 °C and +2 °C recall the Paris Agreement thresholds — **but note** that those targets are defined relative to **1850–1900 pre-industrial**, and this chart uses 1991–2020 or 1995–2014 as its baseline. The rings here are statistical reference markers, not policy-equivalent thresholds.

**Methods.** Same CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 data as P1. For temperature, spiral radius scales at 70 px per 1 °C anomaly (so +2 °C = 140 px outside the baseline ring). For PTOT, radius scales adaptively (70 px per 1 inter-annual σ of the baseline-period anomalies) — this makes the spiral legible regardless of the country's overall rainfall regime, but **radii are not comparable across countries with different σ**. The colour saturates at ~1 standard deviation above/below the baseline (`cFactor = 0.45`) — extreme months can exceed the palette limits but stay at the colour endpoints rather than rendering off-scale.

**Citations.** Hawkins et al. (2017) for the climate-spiral concept; Funk et al. (2015) and Hersbach et al. (2020) for the underlying data. See [References](#references).

lead.en: 12 month wedges around the clock (Jan at top, clockwise), years as concentric rings outward. Cell fill = value or anomaly. Warming visible as colour shift from inner (old) to outer (recent) rings.
lead.fr: 12 month wedges around the clock (Jan at top, clockwise), years as concentric rings outward. Cell fill = value or anomaly. Warming visible as colour shift from inner (old) to outer (recent) rings.

body.en:
**Purpose.** 12 angular wedges (months) × N radial rings (years) coloured by value or anomaly. Reading from inner to outer rings traces the full observational record chronologically. Useful for spotting both seasonal patterns *and* the warming signal in a single compact view.

**How to read it.** A consistent inner-to-outer colour gradient indicates a sustained multi-decadal trend (e.g. cool inner rings → hot outer rings = warming). Rings with heterogeneous colour around the clock signal high interannual variability. Dimmed wedges (fill-opacity 0.15) are months **outside** the selected season — use the **Season preset** dropdown to highlight a season (MAM / JJA / OND / DJF) or pick **Custom** to define start / end months for a non-standard growing-season window.

**Methods.** Same CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 data as P1–P3. Anomalies are departures from the per-month baseline mean over the selected window. Colour scale is diverging (RdBu) in anomaly mode and sequential (Inferno) in absolute mode. For PTOT in **absolute** mode the colour domain is clipped to p5–p95 of the data so a single extremely wet month doesn't compress the rest of the scale. Arcs are rendered with D3's `d3.arc()` generator; month-perimeter labels combine the month name with a compact `μ · ↑max [· ↓min]` summary line.

**Citations.** Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020). See [References](#references).

title.en: P5 — Long-run seasonal statistics (climatology heatmap + table)
title.fr: P5 — Long-run seasonal statistics (climatology heatmap + table)

lead.en: Monthly climate summary for a selected country. **Heatmap view**: year × month grid coloured by anomaly — warmer recent years read red, cooler earlier years blue; white dots mark threshold exceedances. **Table view**: long-run statistics (mean / min / max / interannual σ) across all four variables, filterable by season. TMAX = mean of daily maximum temperatures; TMIN = mean of daily minimum temperatures.
lead.fr: Monthly climate summary for a selected country. **Heatmap view**: year × month grid coloured by anomaly — warmer recent years read red, cooler earlier years blue; white dots mark threshold exceedances. **Table view**: long-run statistics (mean / min / max / interannual σ) across all four variables, filterable by season. TMAX = mean of daily maximum temperatures; TMIN = mean of daily minimum temperatures.

body.en:
**Purpose.** Combines a year × month heatmap with a long-run statistics table for the four core observational variables (TAVG, TMAX, TMIN, PTOT). The heatmap is the visual entry point — patterns of warming, drying, or wet-season variability stand out at a glance. The table provides the numerical backbone (mean, min year, max year, inter-annual σ) for report writing and citation.

**How to read it.** *Heatmap:* vertical colour stripes show year-to-year shifts; horizontal stripes show consistent seasonal cycles; a left-cool / right-warm gradient is the temperature trend. **White dots** mark months with anomaly ≥ +1 °C; **rings** mark ≥ +1.5 °C — these are common framing thresholds for adaptation narratives. For PTOT, dots mark months **wetter than +1σ** (white) and **drier than −1σ** (black ring), with σ computed per month so wet and dry seasons each get their own scale. *Table:* TMAX is the **mean of daily maximum temperatures** (not the warmest temperature on record); TMIN is the **mean of daily minimum temperatures**. PTOT Annual / season row in the table = **total** precipitation, not mean monthly. The σ column header reads `± σ_y` — that's the **inter-annual** standard deviation (year-to-year variability for that month or for the annual total).

**Methods.** CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 monthly admin-0 aggregates. Baseline monthly means computed over the selected window (1991–2020 or 1995–2014). Anomalies = departure from monthly baseline. Heatmap summary row uses the mean of monthly values per year (consistent colour scale across cells); the table's Annual / season row uses the sum for PTOT and the mean for temperature. Min / max in the table = year-of-record extremes for that calendar month.

**Citations.** Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020). See [References](#references).

title.en: CR-097 — When does warming first reach +X °C? (CMIP6 threshold map)
title.fr: CR-097 — When does warming first reach +X °C? (CMIP6 threshold map)

lead.en:
Admin1 choropleth: colour = first 20-year period where ensemble-mean temperature anomaly (vs 1995–2014 baseline) exceeds the chosen threshold. Uses the existing `ensemble_season_timeseries` CMIP6 future-projection parquets — no pipeline wait.

5 colour bins: 2021-40 (earliest) → 2081-2100 (latest) → grey ("threshold not reached by 2100").
lead.fr:
Admin1 choropleth: colour = first 20-year period where ensemble-mean temperature anomaly (vs 1995–2014 baseline) exceeds the chosen threshold. Uses the existing `ensemble_season_timeseries` CMIP6 future-projection parquets — no pipeline wait.

5 colour bins: 2021-40 (earliest) → 2081-2100 (latest) → grey ("threshold not reached by 2100").

body.en:
**Purpose.** For each admin unit, identifies the first 20-year CMIP6 period (2021–2040 / 2041–2060 / 2061–2080 / 2081–2100) in which the multi-model ensemble-mean temperature anomaly exceeds a user-selected threshold (+1 °C / +1.5 °C / +2 °C / +3 °C) relative to the 1995–2014 baseline. Direct support for adaptation-planning questions of the form "when do we expect this district to cross +1.5 °C under SSP2-4.5?".

**How to read it.** **Red** = earliest (2021–2040); **light yellow** = latest (2081–2100); **grey** = threshold not reached by 2100 under the selected scenario. Scenarios matter a lot — compare SSP1-2.6 (strong mitigation) against SSP5-8.5 (high-emission) for the same threshold to see how much mitigation delays the crossing. Caveats: (a) this is the **ensemble-mean** crossing — individual GCMs typically cross the same threshold 1–2 decades earlier or later, which the map understates; (b) for SSP1-2.6 the low-threshold (+1 °C) crossing can be **transient** — the ensemble mean can dip back below later in the century, so the map shows *first* exceedance, not *sustained* exceedance.

**Methods.** Data: NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 `ensemble_season_timeseries` parquets (four files, one per 20-year future period), reading the `mean_anomaly` column for the user-selected variable × season. Threshold crossing = first period in which the ensemble-mean anomaly ≥ threshold. Admin0 values are aggregated client-side as the mean of constituent admin1 means. The NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 v2 ensemble comprises 18 GCMs (ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, CanESM5, CMCC-ESM2, EC-Earth3, EC-Earth3-Veg-LR, GFDL-ESM4, INM-CM4-8, INM-CM5-0, IPSL-CM6A-LR, KACE-1-0-G, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-LM, NorESM2-MM, TaiESM1) — the same ensemble used by the main notebook's Future Projections section.

**Citations.** Thrasher et al. (2022) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6; IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 4 (Lee et al. 2021) for the constrained-projections framing. See [References](#references).

title.en: P6 — Spatial climate change by decade (observational maps)
title.fr: P6 — Spatial climate change by decade (observational maps)

lead.en: Choropleth grid using CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 observational data. **Rows = stats** (mean anomaly vs baseline / linear trend / interannual variability). **Columns = decades**. Each cell shows admin1 or admin0 polygons coloured by that stat for that decade. Trend computed client-side. No pipeline work needed — uses existing `adm1_obs.parquet`.
lead.fr: Choropleth grid using CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 observational data. **Rows = stats** (mean anomaly vs baseline / linear trend / interannual variability). **Columns = decades**. Each cell shows admin1 or admin0 polygons coloured by that stat for that decade. Trend computed client-side. No pipeline work needed — uses existing `adm1_obs.parquet`.

body.en:
**Purpose.** Admin-level choropleth maps comparing observed climate statistics across multiple decades — mean anomaly, variability, and full-record trend — for a selected variable and season. Enables spatial identification of warming / drying / wetting hotspots and sub-national regions of changing variability. Complements the single-country time-series views above by exposing **where** the change is concentrated within a country or region.

**How to read it.** *Decade grid:* compare colour intensity across the columns to track decade-by-decade change. Mean-anomaly panels are relative to the full baseline window; admin1s with decades inside the baseline (e.g. 1990s when baseline = 1991–2020) will show smaller anomalies — that is expected. *Variability panels:* darker shading = higher inter-annual standard deviation in that decade, **independent of trend direction**. Palette is **Purples** (or Viridis in CB mode) so darker ≠ "wetter" — this avoids the colour-meaning conflict for PTOT and SPEI.

*Full-record trend maps* (below the decade grid): show the statistically tested direction of the long-term trend. **Black border / dot** marks Mann-Kendall significance (p < 0.05). For regional views with >80 features, non-significant admin1s are **faded** instead of dotted (dots become unreadable at that density). The decade-grid "Trend (per decade)" stat — when toggled on — uses a simple OLS slope on ≤10-year windows; it is **indicative only**. The full-record map beneath uses **Theil-Sen + Mann-Kendall + TFPW** (trend-free pre-whitening) — the same methodology as the main notebook's Recent Changes section.

**Methods.** Data: CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 `adm1_obs.parquet` (sub-national annual / seasonal aggregates) or `adm0_obs.parquet`. Trend slope: Theil-Sen estimator (median of pairwise slopes — robust to outliers). Significance: non-parametric Mann-Kendall test on TFPW-pre-whitened residuals at α = 0.05 (Yue & Wang 2002). Variability: `d3.deviation` of annual values per decade. Variability trend (in the full-record map): Theil-Sen slope of a 5-year rolling mean-absolute-residual series (detrended to remove mean-shift confound), normalised by baseline σ → %/decade. PTOT variability is suppressed for admin1s with baseline mean < 10 mm/month (arid-zone artefact). SPEI is already a standardised z-score, so its variability trend is intentionally not displayed.

**Citations.** Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020); Yue & Wang (2002); Mann (1945); Kendall (1975); Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010) for the SPEI baseline definition. See [References](#references).

*Full-record trend maps* (below the decade grid): show the statistically tested direction of the long-term trend. **Black border / dot** marks Mann-Kendall significance (p < 0.05). For regional views with >80 features, non-significant admin1s are **faded** instead of dotted (dots become unreadable at that density). The decade-grid "Trend (per decade)" stat — when toggled on — uses a simple OLS slope on ≤10-year windows; it is **indicative only**. The full-record map beneath uses **Theil-Sen + Mann-Kendall + TFPW** (trend-free pre-whitening) — the same methodology as the main notebook's Recent Changes section.

**Methods.** Data: CHIRPS-CHIRTS-ERA5 `adm1_obs.parquet` (sub-national annual / seasonal aggregates) or `adm0_obs.parquet`. Trend slope: Theil-Sen estimator (median of pairwise slopes — robust to outliers). Significance: non-parametric Mann-Kendall test on TFPW-pre-whitened residuals at α = 0.05 (Yue & Wang 2002). Variability: `d3.deviation` of annual values per decade. Variability trend (in the full-record map): Theil-Sen slope of a 5-year rolling mean-absolute-residual series (detrended to remove mean-shift confound), normalised by baseline σ → %/decade. PTOT variability is suppressed for admin1s with baseline mean < 10 mm/month (arid-zone artefact). SPEI is already a standardised z-score, so its variability trend is intentionally not displayed.

**Citations.** Funk et al. (2015); Hersbach et al. (2020); Yue & Wang (2002); Mann (1945); Kendall (1975); Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010) for the SPEI baseline definition. See [References](#references).
